label: Near East
subtitle: Levant, Arabia, Iraq, Iran & Anatolia
about: Cuisines of the Levant, Arabia, Mesopotamia, Iran and Anatolia.

label: Palestinian & Levant
subtitle: Sumac, olive oil, allspice, tahini
about: Centered on Palestine and the southern Levant along the eastern Mediterranean coast and the inland hills around Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, this cuisine belongs to a wider food region shared with Jordan, Lebanon and Syria. Palestinian Arab village and city traditions, Ottoman-era exchange, trade and migration all shaped it; classic dishes include musakhan, maqluba, maftoul and mujaddara. Many foods are shared across the Levant, so these dishes should not automatically be described as uniquely Palestinian.
signature_ingredients: hand-rolled Palestinian wheat granules (مفتول, maftūl) (substitute: pearl couscous for texture only; flavor and production are not equivalent)
roasted green wheat (فريكة, farīka/freekeh) (substitute: bulgur, preferably coarse; less smoky)
jute mallow leaves (ملوخية, mulūkhiyya) (substitute: frozen molokhia if fresh is unavailable; spinach is only a functional substitute and lacks the characteristic texture)
taboon bread (خبز طابون, khubz ṭābūn) (substitute: thick pita or naan; neither reproduces taboon flavor exactly)
gundelia, a seasonal wild thistle used in some Palestinian cooking (عكوب, ʿakkūb) (substitute: artichoke hearts for a rough functional substitute; none is exact)
tips: Store-bought za'atar: commonly contains za'atar-type herb, sumac, sesame and salt. Substitute 1:1 by weight for a homemade za'atar condiment. Because salt varies by brand, calculate salt from the label (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium) for the quantity used, and reduce added recipe salt by that amount.

Baharat or Lebanese seven-spice: Reem Kassis specifically recommends these as convenient substitutes for her family's Palestinian nine-spice, with a slightly different flavor. Use 1:1 by weight for the ground spice quantity; many versions contain no salt, but verify the label. If sodium is 0 mg, salt contribution is 0 g.

Prepared tahini sauce is not the same as plain tahini. If a recipe calls for tahini paste, substitute only plain sesame tahini 1:1 by weight; prepared sauces may already contain lemon, garlic, water and salt. Use the package sodium to calculate salt from label sodium (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium).
pitfalls: Do not call every shared Levantine dish uniquely Palestinian, Lebanese, Syrian or Jordanian; borders are newer than many dishes.
Do not treat za'atar as simply dried thyme: the word can mean the herb itself or a condiment usually combining the herb with sumac, sesame and salt.
Do not make Reem Kassis's family nine-spice a universal Palestinian formula.
Do not add pomegranate molasses, tahini or za'atar to every dish merely to make it seem 'Middle Eastern.'
Do not insert shakshuka as a Palestinian default; it is North African in origin even though versions are now eaten elsewhere.
Do not flatten Gazan cooking into the same profile as Jerusalem or the northern West Bank; Gaza has especially strong seafood, chili, dill and sour traditions.

label: Persian
subtitle: Herbs, saffron, dried lime, sour fruit
about: Persian cooking developed across the Iranian plateau between the Caspian Sea and Persian Gulf, divided by the Alborz and Zagros mountain ranges and containing sharply different climates. Persian-speaking court and urban traditions interacted for centuries with Iran's many regional peoples and with trade routes linking Central Asia, the Caucasus, Mesopotamia and the Indian Ocean. Representative dishes include ghormeh sabzi, fesenjan, chelow kabab and tahchin.
flavors: unripe sour grapes or verjuice (غوره, ghūreh)
sweet_only: dried Damask rose petals (گل محمدی, gol-e moḥammadi)
signature_ingredients: barberries (زرشک, zereshk) (substitute: dried cranberries soaked briefly in lemon juice; sweeter and not equivalent)
fermented dried dairy product, usually reconstituted (کشک, kashk) (substitute: strained Greek yogurt mixed with a little feta for body; flavor is not equivalent)
Persian shallot (موسیر, mūsīr) (substitute: ordinary shallot plus a small amount of garlic)
unripe sour grapes (غوره, ghūreh) (substitute: verjuice if available; otherwise lemon juice diluted slightly with water)
tips: Commercial advieh: formulas vary by dish and producer and may contain cinnamon, cardamom, cumin, rose, nutmeg or other spices. Substitute 1:1 by weight only when the blend is intended for the same dish family; do not treat 'advieh' as one universal formula. If the label shows 0 mg sodium, salt contribution is 0 g; otherwise estimate salt from label sodium (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium).

Prepared or frozen ghormeh-sabzi herb mixtures can replace the same prepared herb component by weight, but verify whether they are raw, fried or salted before substitution. For a salted product, calculate salt from label sodium (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium).

Bottled pomegranate molasses may replace homemade reduced pomegranate concentrate 1:1 by weight as a starting point, but sweetness and acidity vary substantially by brand; adjust sourness rather than adding sugar automatically.
pitfalls: Do not make every Persian dish sweet, floral or saffron-heavy.
Do not make Persian food generically hot with large amounts of chile; classic seasoning is usually aromatic rather than strongly fiery.
Do not replace dried lime with fresh lime and claim the flavor is identical.
Do not omit the parboil-and-steam process when a classic chelow texture is intended.
Do not assume all Iranian regional cuisines are identical to a Tehran-centered Persian canon; Caspian, Azeri, Kurdish, southern and other regional traditions differ substantially.
Do not use the word 'tahdig' for any crispy rice without preserving the deliberate bottom-crust technique.
substitutes: dried limes (لیمو عمانی, līmū-ye ʿomānī): fresh lime juice plus a small amount of lime zest; misses the fermented earthy bitterness

label: Turkish
subtitle: Pul biber, yogurt, sumac, herbs
about: Turkish cuisine spans Anatolia between the Black Sea, Aegean and Mediterranean and includes Istanbul at the Bosporus, with major regional differences from the southeast to the Aegean coast. It was shaped by Anatolian foodways, Turkic migrations, Seljuk and Ottoman kitchens, and long interaction with Balkan, Caucasian, Mediterranean and Middle Eastern communities. Representative dishes include mantı, dolma and sarma, kebabs, börek and olive-oil vegetable dishes.
signature_ingredients: thin rolled flatbread or pastry sheets (yufka) (substitute: lavash for flatbread uses or phyllo for layered pastry uses; neither is universally interchangeable)
fermented dried grain-yogurt soup base (tarhana) (substitute: none)
highly seasoned cured sausage (sucuk) (substitute: a garlicky beef sausage; chorizo is only a rough functional substitute and has a different spice profile)
pressed, cured beef coated with çemen (pastırma) (substitute: bresaola plus garlic and fenugreek for a rough functional substitute; none is exact)
Turkish cut egg noodles (erişte) (substitute: wide supermarket egg noodles)
tips: Biber salçası: commercial pepper paste can replace homemade pepper paste 1:1 by weight as a starting point. Many jars are salted, so calculate salt from label sodium (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium) from the nutrition label for the weight used and subtract that salt from the recipe.

Domates salçası: concentrated supermarket tomato paste can usually replace Turkish tomato paste 1:1 by weight, but concentration varies; adjust liquid and browning rather than assuming identical strength. Account for labeled sodium (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium).

Nar ekşisi: use a product whose main ingredient is pomegranate rather than a generic sweet 'pomegranate sauce' when classic sourness is intended. Substitute 1:1 by weight as a starting point; sweetness, acidity and salt vary by product.

Köfte baharı: commercial meatball-spice blends vary; one documented traditional formulation combines coriander, black pepper, cloves, bay and wild thyme. Use 1:1 by weight only in recipes that actually call for köfte seasoning. If salted, derive salt from the label (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium).
pitfalls: Do not reduce Turkish cuisine to kebab, hummus and baklava; vegetable dishes, legumes, grains, soups, yogurt dishes and regional foods are equally important.
Do not describe modern Turkish cuisine as deriving solely from Ottoman palace cooking.
Do not add pomegranate molasses to every Turkish dish; it is particularly important in southern and southeastern traditions.
Do not add fenugreek to ordinary Turkish recipes merely because çemen is traditional; its use is specialized and regional.
Do not assume kekik always means the exact same botanical herb as supermarket English thyme.
Do not treat all pul biber as Aleppo pepper; Turkish red-pepper flakes vary substantially by region and processing, and isot is a distinct Şanlıurfa pepper product.
Do not make every meze tahini-based; yogurt, vegetables, legumes, olive oil, herbs and seafood also form major meze families.

label: Yemeni
subtitle: Hawaij, fenugreek foam, zhoug, flatbreads
about: Yemeni home cooking spans the terraced western highlands around Sana'a, the hot Red Sea coastal plain of Tihama, the southern port of Aden, and the eastern desert wadis of Hadhramaut. Summer monsoon rains and ancient mountain terraces sustained sorghum, millet, wheat, and coffee, while Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade connected Yemen with India, East Africa, and Southeast Asia alongside centuries of Jewish and Ottoman exchange. Everyday meals center on warm spice blends, clay-oven or skillet flatbreads, whipped fenugreek, chili-herb pastes, smoked clarified butter, and honey, with representative dishes including saltah, fahsa, mandi, and zhurbian.
sweet_only: mainly in Adeni halwa and festive sweets (rosewater)
prized jujube honey poured mainly over bint al-sahn, areeka, and masoub (Sidr honey)
signature_ingredients: sorghum flour and grain (ذرة, dhura) (substitute: millet flour or whole-wheat flour; earthy flavor differs)
lahooh (لحوح, spongy fermented flatbread) (substitute: east African injera, or a thin fermented pancake cooked on one side only)
malawah (ملوح, flaky ghee-layered flatbread) (substitute: uncooked frozen plain South Asian paratha)
qishr (قشر, dried coffee cherry husks) (substitute: specialty cascara tea; none in standard US supermarkets)
lakhm (لخم, Hadhrami cured dried shark) (substitute: salted dried cod, soaked well; flavor is milder)
wazif (وزف, sun-dried baby sardines) (substitute: asian dried anchovies or rinsed oil-packed anchovies; intensity differs)
tips: Commercial savory hawaij spice blend: usually contains ground cumin, black pepper, turmeric, and cardamom, sometimes with coriander or cloves. Substitute 1:1 by weight for homemade savory hawaij. Most pure spice blends contain 0 mg sodium (0 g salt), though salted blends exist (uncertain across brands on whether an unlabeled mix is salted); check the nutrition label and reduce added recipe salt by about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium for the weight used.

Prepared refrigerated or jarred zhoug paste: usually contains cilantro, hot green chiles, garlic, vegetable oil, salt, and warm spices such as cumin and cardamom. Swap 1:1 by weight for homemade green sahawiq, noting that commercial pastes are often milder and oilier than mortar-pounded versions. Sodium varies widely by producer — roughly 250 to 550 mg sodium per 100 g, or about 0.6 to 1.4 g salt per 100 g (uncertain across brands, brand-varying) — so read the label and reduce added dish salt by about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium.

Commercial meat bouillon cubes or powder as a shortcut for slow-simmered meat broth (maraq): usually contain salt, yeast extract or hydrolyzed protein, fat, and onion or spice flavorings, lacking the gelatin and roasted-bone depth of homemade maraq. Reconstitute by weight per package directions, and reduce added recipe salt by about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium on the label (sodium content varies substantially by brand, approximate).
pitfalls: Do not default to Levantine za'atar, sumac, or pomegranate molasses in Yemeni recipes; everyday Yemeni cooking leans on hawaij, whipped fenugreek (hulba), and chili-herb paste (sahawiq).
Do not conflate Yemeni mandi with Gulf kabsa; classic Hadhrami mandi suspends lightly spiced meat over basmati rice with wood smoke and drippings rather than simmering rice in a tomato-based broth.
Do not omit whipped fenugreek foam (hulba) from saltah or fahsa, and do not boil dry ground fenugreek straight into the stew without soaking and draining or it turns harshly bitter.
Do not treat zhoug as strictly green or solely Israeli; Yemeni sahawiq includes red chile, cheese (bil-jibn), and dried-sardine (wazif) versions alongside the green cilantro paste.
Do not assume Yemeni flatbreads are standard pita; lahooh is a one-sided fermented sorghum-or-mixed-grain crepe, and traditional Yemeni malawah is ghee-laminated rather than margarine-fried.
pantry: all-purpose and whole-wheat or sorghum flour
plain yogurt and lemons or limes

label: Iraqi
subtitle: Dried lime, tamarind, baharat, date syrup
about: Spanning the Tigris and Euphrates river plains from Baghdad down to the Shatt al-Arab marshes and Basra near the Persian Gulf, and rising north toward Mosul and the Zagros mountains of Iraqi Kurdistan, Iraqi home cooking is shaped by fertile riverbeds, northern highlands, and date-palm groves. Rooted in ancient Mesopotamian foodways and medieval Abbasid Baghdad, it reflects centuries of Arab, Kurdish, Turkmen, Assyrian, Iraqi Jewish, Ottoman, Persian, and Indian Ocean trade influences, balancing warm spice blends against pronounced sour and sweet-sour accents. Representative dishes include wood-roasted Tigris carp (masgouf), sweet-and-sour mixed-vegetable dolma, filled cracked-wheat or rice kubba, slow-roasted lamb and rice quzi, and layered eggplant casserole tepsi baytinijan.
flavors: dried black lime (نومي بصرة, noomi basra)
signature_ingredients: anbar / Iraqi amber rice (تمن عنبر, timman anbar) (substitute: aged basmati rice mixed with a small portion of jasmine rice for fragrance; texture differs)
fine cracked wheat for kubba shells (جريش, jarish) (substitute: fine-grind bulgur wheat; soak briefly before kneading)
fermented dried yogurt-wheat paste or powder (كشك / ترخينة, kashk / tarhana) (substitute: strained Greek yogurt whisked with a little cooked bulgur for body, though it lacks fermented tang)
Iraqi diamond-shaped hearth bread (صمون, samoon) (substitute: crusty ciabatta rolls or thick pita pockets)
split or shelled fava beans (باقلاء, bagilla) (substitute: peeled broad beans or frozen lima beans as a rough stand-in)
whole freshwater carp for masgouf (سمك شبوط / كطان, shabbut / kattan) (substitute: butterflied whole sea bass, red snapper, or trout)
crushed sour white citric acid crystals (لمندوزي, lamindozi) (substitute: fresh lemon juice, noting that it adds acidity with more liquid)
tips: Commercial Iraqi baharat or Middle Eastern seven-spice blends: usually contain black pepper, cumin, coriander, allspice, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and nutmeg (though Levantine seven-spice mixes often omit cumin and turmeric or lean heavier on allspice). Swap 1:1 by weight for homemade Iraqi baharat, adding a pinch of cumin and turmeric if using a Levantine blend. Pure spice blends typically contain 0 mg sodium (0 g salt), though seasoned packets with added salt vary by brand [uncertain across brands]; check the nutrition panel and subtract about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium from the recipe.

Jarred amba (pickled mango sauce): usually contains green mango, water, salt, vinegar or citric acid, fenugreek, turmeric, mustard, and chili. Commercial jars commonly carry roughly 2,200 to 2,500 mg sodium per 100 g (about 5.5 to 6.3 g salt per 100 g, or roughly 0.8 to 0.9 g salt per 15 g tablespoon, though levels vary by brand [uncertain across brands]). Use directly as a condiment or swap 1:1 by weight into marinades while reducing added recipe salt by about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium shown on the label.

Commercial tamarind paste or concentrate: usually contains tamarind pulp and water, though some jars add salt or sugar. Pure unsalted tamarind concentrate contains only trace natural sodium (roughly 30 to 50 mg sodium per 100 g, under 0.15 g salt), whereas salted pastes vary by manufacturer [uncertain across brands]. Swap 1:1 by weight for strained homemade tamarind pulp liquid of similar thickness, adjusting water and sweetness to taste and reducing added recipe salt by about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium if salted.

Bottled pomegranate molasses and canned tomato paste: pomegranate molasses usually contains concentrated pomegranate juice (sometimes with sugar and citric acid) and typically carries 0 mg sodium (0 g salt), though sweetness and tartness vary sharply by brand [uncertain across brands]; swap 1:1 by weight for homemade reduced pomegranate juice and taste before adjusting sourness. Unsalted tomato paste carries roughly 60 mg sodium per 100 g (about 0.15 g salt), whereas salted commercial tomato paste varies by brand [uncertain across brands]; swap 1:1 by weight for cooked-down tomato puree and subtract about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium from the label.

Commercial beef or lamb bouillon cubes (sometimes used as a modern shortcut in home stews and rice): usually contain salt, hydrolyzed proteins or yeast extract, fat, starch, and onion or garlic flavoring, with high sodium that varies widely by brand [uncertain across brands]. Dissolve in hot water according to package directions to replace homemade meat stock by weight, and withhold added salt until tasting, counting about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium from the package label.
pitfalls: Do not treat Iraqi dolma as identical to Levantine or Turkish olive-oil dolma; classic Iraqi dolma usually combines multiple vegetables in one pot and leans distinctly sweet-and-sour from pomegranate molasses, tamarind, or citric acid.

Do not assume Iraqi baharat is the same as Levantine allspice-only bahar or Gulf bzar; Iraqi baharat is typically black-pepper-forward with cumin, coriander, allspice, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and nutmeg.

Do not flatten Iraq into Baghdad alone or erase regional contrasts, such as Basra's tamarind, dates, and Gulf seafood, Mosul's flat disc kubba and fermented kashk, and Kurdish mountain herbs, sumac, and dairy.

Do not substitute Indian garam masala or curry powder into Iraqi biryani, which usually relies on sweet-warm Iraqi spices, vermicelli, potatoes, peas, raisins, and fried nuts rather than chilies or coconut.
Do not claim masgouf can only be made with wild Tigris carp or ignore how home cooks adapt the split, turmeric-and-tamarind-basted technique in standard ovens and broilers.
pantry: dried chickpeas or white navy beans
ground baharat spice blend and turmeric
